How Banks Say You Should Dispose of Metal Credit Cards

by Joe H. October 12, 2026
by Joe H. October 12, 2026
188
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 5:49
Instaread

Metal credit cards aren’t unusual anymore. Once reserved mostly for ultra-premium cards, they’re now offered across a wide range of products from American Express, Chase, Capital One, Citi, Bilt and others.

That creates a problem plastic cards never really had.

When a plastic credit card expires or gets replaced, you can cut it up with scissors or run it through a credit-card shredder. Metal cards are a different story. They’re much harder to destroy, and trying to cut one with ordinary scissors can damage the scissors—or possibly you.

So what should you do with an old metal credit card?

Fortunately, some issuers now provide specific instructions.

Capital One

Capital One makes this one easy.

If you’re replacing a metal Capital One card, the bank says the replacement card will come with a return envelope for the old metal card.

Capital One specifically says not to cut metal cards. Instead, put the old card in the provided envelope and send it back so the bank can dispose of it properly.

The same guidance appears on Capital One’s page about expired credit cards. Metal cards can be mailed back using the prepaid return envelope included with the replacement.

So if you’ve just received a new Venture or Venture X, don’t throw away everything in the package before checking for the return envelope.

American Express

American Express also uses prepaid return envelopes for metal cards.

When a metal card is replaced or renewed, Amex says the package includes a postage-paid envelope that can be used to return the old card for destruction.

If you no longer have the envelope, you’ll need to request another return option from American Express.

For U.S. cardmembers, Amex has also said in some replacement situations that it can send a prepaid return envelope or provide a mailing address if you’d rather pay postage yourself.

So the easiest answer with an Amex metal card is to save the envelope that comes with the new one.

Chase

Chase doesn’t publish quite as convenient a procedure, but it does give clear guidance about what not to do.

Chase says metal credit cards should be returned to the card issuer for safe disposal.

Its guidance specifically says not to simply throw an intact card into the trash or recycling bin.

Unlike Capital One and American Express, Chase doesn’t promise on its public page that a prepaid return envelope will automatically arrive with every replacement card.

So if you have an old Sapphire Preferred, Sapphire Reserve, United Club Card or another metal Chase card and don’t already have a return envelope, that’s when you’ll need to contact Chase to arrange the return.

Citi

Citi has several metal cards, including premium AAdvantage cards and the Citi Strata Elite.

This is one issuer where the public instructions aren’t especially helpful.

Citi doesn’t appear to have a current public page explaining exactly how cardholders should dispose of its metal cards.

The practical option is to request a return envelope or return instructions from Citi using the number on the back of the card.

That’s not as satisfying as Capital One mailing you an envelope automatically, but until Citi publishes a formal process, I wouldn’t recommend mailing the card to an address found in an old forum post or years-old article.

Bilt

Bilt’s current Blue, Obsidian and Palladium cards are made of stainless steel.

Column N.A. issues the cards, and Cardless services them.

Unlike Capital One or American Express, Bilt doesn’t appear to publish instructions for returning or recycling an old metal card.

Cardless has a cardholder support portal, but I couldn’t find a published procedure for disposing of a Bilt card.

So this is another case where you’ll need to contact Bilt/Cardless support and ask for the current return instructions.

I wouldn’t assume the card can simply be dropped into household recycling. A stainless steel credit card still contains a chip, magnetic stripe and personal information that should be dealt with before disposal.

Can You Destroy A Metal Card Yourself?

I wouldn’t. But some people have tried and showed the results online.

Regular scissors won’t do much against most metal cards. Heavy-duty tin snips or metal shears can cut some, but laminated cards made from layers of metal and plastic can be surprisingly stubborn. This can also be dangerous for a first DIY attempt.

Also, don’t try burning the card, melting it or putting it through a household shredder. Chase specifically warns against exposing cards to extreme temperatures, and most household shredders aren’t designed to shred metal.

And before destroying any card, make sure you’ve activated the replacement and no longer need the old one.

What About Recycling?

This is where metal cards are more complicated than they look.

A credit card isn’t just a flat piece of stainless steel. It may contain plastic layers, an EMV chip, an antenna for contactless payments and other materials that aren’t meant for normal curbside recycling.

Final Thoughts

Metal cards have become much more common, but getting rid of one still isn’t as simple as cutting up an old plastic Visa.

The good news is that some issuers have made the process reasonably painless.

Capital One sends a prepaid return envelope with replacement metal cards. American Express does much the same thing. Chase tells cardholders to return metal cards to the issuer, although you may need to request the return method yourself.

Citi and Bilt/Cardless are the weak spots. Neither appears to provide detailed public disposal instructions, so for those cards you really do have to contact support.

Sometimes the envelope is already sitting in the box with your replacement card.

[Note from Sharon: I still have a better idea. Stop using metal cards. They’re heavy and much more of a PITA to properly dispose of than their plastic counterparts.]
